title: Pre-Trained Vision-Language Model Selection and Reuse for Downstream Tasks

contributions.purpose: Motivate the (largely neglected) problem of selecting a pre-trained VLM per downstream task, by showing no single VLM dominates across tasks or even across classes within a task.
contributions.mechanism: Empirical measurement of many open-clip VLMs across several downstream tasks and across classes within a task, comparing per-task and per-class strengths.
contributions.evaluation: Qualitative: Figure 1 shows each VLM has distinct strengths, no model outperforms all others on every task, and models weak on general tasks can surpass stronger ones on specific downstream tasks/classes.
contributions.domain: Vision-Language Models / model selection for visual classification
contributions.source_quote: We highlight that the performance of pre-trained VLM varies across different downstream tasks and even among classes within the same task. Therefore, it is important to study the VLM selection problem which is usually neglected by related researchers.

contributions.purpose: Enable data- and compute-efficient, scalable selection and reuse of VLMs without evaluating every candidate on the target task.
contributions.mechanism: Model Label Learning (MLL) paradigm with three modules: model labeling (pre-test each VLM on a semantic graph of >9000 visual concepts to assign a task-independent label), model selection (caption-based similarity matching target classes to semantic-graph nodes), and model reuse (per-class top-k ensemble taking highest-confidence prediction). Labeling is target-task-independent so it scales with hub size.
contributions.evaluation: On the introduced benchmark (49 VLMs, 17 datasets) MLL achieves state-of-the-art model-selection performance and grows with hub scale; per-class best-single-model reuse (k=1) already outperforms baselines on most tasks.
contributions.domain: Vision-Language Models / model selection and reuse
contributions.source_quote: We propose a novel paradigm called Model Label Learning, which encompasses the processes of model labeling, selection, and reuse. This paradigm is both time- and data-efficient, and highly scalable. It can give birth to new VLM model hubs, which can make it easier for users to select and reuse VLM to solve their tasks.

contributions.purpose: Provide a standardized way to evaluate VLM selection and reuse methods, which previously lacked benchmarks.
contributions.mechanism: Construction of a benchmark with 49 pre-trained VLMs and 17 target datasets, providing ground-truth model ranking per task, plus a semantic graph of >9000 visual concepts for labeling.
contributions.evaluation: Benchmark of 49 VLMs and 17 target datasets with per-task ground-truth rankings; used to validate effectiveness and scalability of MLL.
contributions.source_quote: We introduce a new benchmark for evaluating pre-trained VLM selection and reuse methods, contributing to the advancement of research in this field. Experimental results validate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposal for selecting and reusing VLMs.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Zohar et al. (2023) is the first study to focus on VLM selection, proposing to evaluate VLM performance using textual information. However, their selection strategy heavily depends on the models' ground-truth performance on large-scale datasets, such as ImageNet. When models excel on large-scale datasets but under-perform on specific tasks, selection strategy effectiveness drops, as shown later in our experiments.

Learnware (Zhou & Tan, 2022) is a novel paradigm that explores more effective model selection by constructing specifications to describe the capabilities of the model, closely aligning with our idea of model labeling... However, learnware requires training data to construct specifications. Considering the scale of VLM pre-trained datasets, it is unrealistic to construct specifications for learnware to select models due to limited time and computational resources.

previous works on model selection (Tran et al., 2019; You et al., 2021) primarily focus on single-modal models, making them unsuitable for VLM selection since they only handle either image or text output and cannot incorporate data from the other modality.

notes: Trade-off/negative result explicitly reported: on weak model hubs (e.g. CLEVR-D, DMLab) the ensemble reuse introduces more noise than benefit, so single-model-per-class (k=1) is better; likewise for few-class datasets (PCam, MNIST). Baseline LOVM/ModelGPT is shown to fail exactly when its ImageNet-based prior fails. Positioned as extending the learnware model-specification idea to the training-data-free VLM setting. Stated limitation: only VLMs and visual classification covered.
